newsitem.title: BULGARIA: POLL GIVES BULGARIA'S UDF 62 PCT SUPPORT.
newsitem.headline: POLL GIVES BULGARIA'S UDF 62 PCT SUPPORT.

text.p: Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) and its coalition allies would win up to 62 percent support if general elections were held now, an opinion poll showed on Friday.

"If early elections were held now the United Democratic Forces (UDF plus allies) would win maximum support between 60 and 62 percent," Jivko Georgiev of the Bulgarian branch of Gallup polling agency told a news conference.
The UDF led month-long mass protests in January which forced the ruling ex-communist Socialist Party to stand down. Elections have been called 20 months ahead of schedule.

All Bulgarian political parties have pledged their support for a tough reform programme agreed by the interim cabinet and the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the shattered economy over the next years.
Support for the UDF could fall to a minimum of 55 percent as enthusiasm from street protests gives way to everyday economic hardship, said Georgiev.

The survey showed 16 to 17 percent support for the Socialists, who lost power after failing to cope with a deep economic crisis. They won parliamentary elections in December 1994 but lost support as the economy worsened.
Georgiev said the Socialists could gain a further three percent from voters who are reluctant to admit their affiliation to interviewers.
Some 40 parties and coalitions will take part in Bulgaria's general election on April 19, but Georgiev saw only four entering parliament.

Two new parties are seen jumping the four percent of total votes barrier required for admission in the assembly, the National Salvation Union (NSU) with six to seven percent, and the Euro-Left with 4.5 to six percent, said Georgiev.
The Euro-Left has attracted Socialists who were disappointed with the previous government.

The NSU groups the ethnic Turkish Movement for Rights and Freedoms, which split from the UDF coalition at the last moment, an agrarian party and the Liberal Democratic Alternative set up by former president Zhelyu Zhelev.
Gallup-Bulgaria estimates show that 74 percent of eligible voters will vote, 16 percent of those polled have said they will not vote and 10 percent are undecided.
The Bulgarian Business Block, which styled itself at the presidential elections as an alternative to the two main parties, is seen scoring 3.6 to five percent.

The lacklustre election campaign has attracted little attention from voters so far, fewer than 25 percent of the voters follow debates broadcast on TV several times a week, said Georgiev. Interest is expected to pick up as the campaign gets more interesting towards its end, he added.
